hints: Look carefully at the two chambers named in the question. Which valve sits directly between the right atrium and the right ventricle?
Remember the golden rule of valves: blood pushes a valve shut when pressure behind it is higher, to stop backflow. What would high ventricle pressure do to that valve?
walkthrough:
**Find the valve in between**

Think of the heart as two sides with doors between rooms. The door between the right atrium (top) and right ventricle (bottom) is the right atrioventricular valve, also called the tricuspid valve.

This is the only valve directly affected by those two pressures.

**Apply the pressure rule**

Valves are passive flaps, they respond to pressure differences. When atrial pressure is higher, blood flows forward and the AV valve is open.

When ventricular pressure becomes higher, blood tries to push backwards, and that back-pressure slams the AV valve shut to prevent backflow.

**Link to the cardiac cycle**

This moment is the start of ventricular systole (contraction). The right AV valve closes first, giving the first heart sound. Only later, when ventricle pressure exceeds artery pressure, do the semilunar valves open.

So the direct result is closure of the right atrioventricular valve.

options.A: This is on the left side of the heart, between left ventricle and aorta. It is not affected by right-sided pressures.
options.B: The pulmonary semilunar valve will open, not close, when right ventricle pressure rises high enough. Closure happens later during diastole.
options.C: This is the left AV (bicuspid/mitral) valve. It responds to left atrium and left ventricle pressures, not right-sided pressures.
options.D: Correct. Higher pressure in the right ventricle than the right atrium pushes blood back and closes the right atrioventricular valve to prevent backflow.
